spans.assertion: the analysis examined whether referees are more likely to give dark-skin-toned players red cards than light-skin-toned players, using 115,457 player-referee dyads for 1,419 players across four European leagues in the 2012-2013 season

dark-skin-toned players have a 0.194 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skin-toned players after adjusting for confounders (95% CI 0.020-0.389, p=0.045), about a 16% relative increase
the adjusted odds ratio for receiving a red card is 1.165 (95% CI 1.003-1.353, p=0.046), i.e. 16.5% higher odds for dark-skin-toned players
the adjusted risk difference estimate is 0.194 percentage points, 95% CI (0.020, 0.389), two-sided p=0.0449
the risk difference was computed by comparing predicted red-card probability if all players were set to dark-skinned versus all set to light-skinned, holding other characteristics constant
the 95% CI for the risk difference excludes zero, taken as evidence of a positive association between dark skin tone and red-card probability
baseline red-card probability is 1.22% for light-skin players and 1.41% for dark-skin players, a 15.9% relative increase
despite the small absolute difference, the relative increase is judged substantively meaningful and suggestive of systematic differential treatment
the adjusted odds ratio is 1.165, 95% CI (1.003, 1.353), p=0.0457
the odds-ratio CI barely excludes the null value of 1.0, indicating only marginal statistical significance, consistent with the primary risk-difference result
the unit of analysis was defined as the player-referee dyad
the analysis sample comprised 115,457 dyads representing 1,419 unique players
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator of whether any red card was given within a dyad, aggregated across all games that player-referee pair encountered
dark skin was defined as a skin-tone rating of 0.5 or higher on the 0-1 scale
players classified as dark-skinned made up 23.2% of the sample
players classified as light-skinned (rating below 0.5) made up 77.1% of the sample
skin tone was measured as the average of two independent raters who coded player photos on a scale from 0 (very light) to 1 (very dark)
inter-rater reliability was Pearson r=0.923, with 99.9% agreement within 0.25 points
21,407 dyads (14.7% of the original 146,028) were excluded for missing skin-tone ratings, i.e. players without available photos
9,164 dyads (7.4%) were excluded for missing covariate data, primarily missing player position
the final analysis sample was 115,457 dyads, 79.1% of the original data
85.3% of dyads had skin-tone data available, treated as reasonable coverage despite the photo-based exclusions
missing covariate data was minimal, under 8%, and primarily due to missing position information

the regression model adjusted for six confounders: log number of games in the dyad, player position (12 categories), league country, player height and weight, referee-country implicit bias score, and referee-country explicit bias score

a rationale was given for each covariate: games captures opportunity, position captures aggressive play, league/country captures playing styles and referee practices, physical characteristics relate to play style, and referee bias measures capture referee-level attitudes

individual referee fixed effects, player-specific aggressive-play history, match-level factors, and yellow-card history were not included as covariates; referee fixed effects were dropped because 152 referee-country categories caused singularity, and the others were unavailable data
the games variable was natural-log transformed to reduce right skew
games had a mean of 3.0 and a range of 1-47
skin tone was used as a binary variable (>=0.5 vs <0.5) in the primary analysis
a continuous-skin-tone sensitivity analysis was also conducted
red cards were dichotomized into any vs. none
the original red-card variable counted 0, 1, or 2 red cards
a logistic regression was fit with the binary skin-tone predictor and the covariates

adjusted risk difference was estimated via G-computation/marginal standardization: two counterfactual datasets were created (all dyads set to dark_skin=1 and all set to dark_skin=0), probabilities were predicted from the fitted model under each, and the risk difference was the mean predicted probability under 'all dark' minus 'all light'

a parametric bootstrap with 1,000 iterations was used for the confidence interval: parameter vectors were simulated from a multivariate normal distribution using the estimated coefficients and variance-covariance matrix, the risk difference was recomputed for each simulated draw, and the 95% CI was taken from the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles
the adjusted odds ratio was taken directly from the logistic regression coefficient for dark_skin, with a Wald-type 95% CI from the normal approximation

cluster-robust standard errors were used at the player level (1,419 clusters), reasoned as necessary because each player appears in multiple dyads with different referees and so observations are not independent
player fixed effects were not used because they would remove all between-player variation, including skin tone
referee-country fixed effects were not included because 152 categories caused model singularity; aggregated bias scores were used instead
position and league were treated as categorical fixed effects
no survey weights or inverse-probability weights were applied; each dyad was weighted equally regardless of number of games, with sensitivity to that choice addressed via the log-games covariate

spans.assertion: unadjusted red-card rates were 1.230% for light-skin and 1.343% for dark-skin players, an unadjusted risk difference of 0.113 percentage points

the adjusted risk-difference estimate (0.194pp) is larger than the unadjusted estimate (0.113pp), interpreted as confounders having partially masked the true association, consistent with dark-skin players more often playing in positions or leagues with fewer red cards
standardized differences between skin-tone groups showed good balance for log(games) and weight, and slight imbalance for height, mean IAT score, and mean explicit bias score
dark-skin players are slightly taller and play in countries with lower average implicit/explicit racial bias, and adjusting for these factors strengthens the observed association
model diagnostics: McFadden pseudo R-squared of 0.0951, log-likelihood of -7067.09, and the model converged successfully
variance inflation factors were all below 3
small differences in rates can accumulate to a meaningful disparate impact over a season
the effect is in the hypothesized direction: dark-skin-toned players receive more red cards
the result meets the pre-specified significance threshold (p=0.045<0.05), though the CI lower bound (0.020) being close to zero indicates only marginal significance
sensitivity analyses were conducted and their consistency is said to strengthen confidence in the result

over a season a player with 30 games would have about 0.4 percentage points higher cumulative red-card probability if dark-skinned versus light-skinned, which at the league level (2,053 players) translates to observable disparities in disciplinary outcomes
21,407 dyads (15%) were excluded for lacking a player photo, which may limit generalizability since excluded players may be less prominent or from certain leagues
an 85% retention rate and inclusion of major-league players is said to mitigate the selection-bias concern from missing photos
high inter-rater reliability (r=0.923) is said to support consistent measurement despite skin tone being coded from photos subject to lighting, quality, and rater perception
a continuous sensitivity analysis is said to confirm a dose-response relationship, supporting the robustness of the binary dichotomization
aggregating red cards across all games in a dyad does not capture game-specific context such as score, time, or match importance
actual aggressive play or foul severity could not be observed, only referee decisions
adjustment for position is said to capture defensive roles
adjustment for yellow cards is said to show a similar pattern, though this analysis is not shown
implicit bias measures are said to suggest referee-level factors are at play
no data was available on match score, game importance, or referee characteristics beyond country
